content: Conditional recommendations are made only under specific circumstances. These conditions arise due to factors such as the lack of high-quality evidence, imprecision in outcome estimates, uncertainty about patient preferences and the value they place on outcomes, minimal benefits compared to potential harms, and benefits that may not justify the associated costs, including implementation costs. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) carefully discussed and agreed on the wording of recommendations, ensuring the use of non-stigmatizing language. These recommendations also incorporate human rights considerations, as outlined in the United Nations Principles and Guidelines for eliminating discrimination against individuals affected by leprosy and their families, with special attention to women, children, and other vulnerable populations. All decisions were reached after thorough discussions of the proposed recommendations, including their strengths and any conditions that needed to be attached. Disagreements were resolved through evidence review and informal consensus facilitated by the Chair and Co-Chair during face-to-face meetings. Evidence-to-recommendation tables were developed during the GDG meeting, with only minor editorial changes made afterward. These tables were circulated to all GDG members for endorsement and finalization. A draft of the guidelines was shared with GDG members during consultations with the Evidence Review Group (ERG), and the final version was approved by all GDG members before submission to the Guidelines Review Committee (GRC). Although vaccinations could potentially prevent leprosy, the World Health Organization (WHO) regulations require that the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) formulate all vaccination (immunoprophylaxis) recommendations. Therefore, while the GDG reviewed evidence on vaccinations, they did not formulate recommendations. Instead, their findings were shared with the SAGE BCG working group to inform its recommendations. Diagnosis of Leprosy The diagnosis of leprosy is recommended to be based on clinical examination, with or without slit-skin smears or pathological examination of biopsies. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Diagnosis in current practice relies on identifying at least one of the three cardinal signs: (1) definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch, (2) thickened or enlarged peripheral nerves with loss of sensation and/or muscle weakness supplied by that nerve, or (3) the presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear. However, slit-skin smears require technical expertise for collection, fixation, staining, and interpretation. The early clinical stages of leprosy, particularly milder forms (paucibacillary or PB leprosy), are the most challenging to diagnose. Tests such as ELISA and lateral flow assays show low accuracy for PB leprosy. While PCR-based assays using tissue specimens demonstrate higher sensitivity and specificity, they are difficult to perform in most field settings due to the lack of standardization, commercial availability, and the need for technical expertise. PCR assays using urine and blood samples are less invasive alternatives but have low sensitivity. Diagnosis of Leprosy Infection in Asymptomatic Contacts Currently, there is no test recommended by the GDG to diagnose latent leprosy infection among asymptomatic contacts. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Evaluating potential tests for Mycobacterium leprae infection requires long-term follow-up to determine their predictive utility. While a test to identify latent infection would be useful for preventive interventions, available tests lack sufficient accuracy to recommend their use. Treatment Regimens for Leprosy The GDG recommends the same three-drug regimen (rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine) for all leprosy patients. The treatment duration is six months for PB leprosy and 12 months for multibacillary (MB) leprosy. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. The current multidrug therapy (MDT) for PB leprosy includes rifampicin and dapsone for six months, while MB leprosy treatment includes rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone for 12 months. MDT is distributed in blister packs free of cost, with specific packs for adults and children. The GDG considered the potential benefits of using a uniform MDT (UMDT) regimen for all leprosy patients, which could simplify treatment logistics, reduce the impact of misclassification of leprosy cases, and improve clinical outcomes for PB leprosy patients. Evidence suggests that a three-drug regimen for PB leprosy may result in better clinical outcomes compared to a two-drug regimen. However, for MB leprosy, there is insufficient evidence to support shortening the treatment duration from 12 to six months, as this may increase the risk of relapse. Treatment for Drug-Resistant Leprosy For patients with rifampicin-resistant leprosy, the GDG recommends treatment with at least two second-line drugs (clarithromycin, minocycline, or a quinolone such as ofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin) plus clofazimine daily for six months, followed by clofazimine and one second-line drug daily for an additional 18 months. In cases of rifampicin and ofloxacin resistance, quinolones should not be used, and the recommended regimen includes clarithromycin, minocycline, and clofazimine. These recommendations are based on expert opinion, as no direct evidence was available. Drug resistance in leprosy is a growing concern, with cases of resistance to rifampicin, dapsone, and quinolones reported in several high-burden countries. Patients found to have resistance to rifampicin, either alone or in combination with dapsone resistance, should restart a full course of second-line treatment regardless of clinical outcomes with MDT. Pharmacovigilance is essential to monitor adverse events, including cardiac risks associated with clarithromycin, minocycline, and quinolones. Prevention of Leprosy Through Chemoprophylaxis The GDG recommends the use of single-dose rifampicin (SDR) as preventive treatment for contacts of leprosy patients (adults and children aged two years and above), after excluding leprosy and tuberculosis (TB) and ensuring the absence of contraindications. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. Leprosy prevention is preferable to treatment after clinical presentation, as it reduces disease spread and associated social consequences. An RCT demonstrated that SDR reduced the risk of leprosy by 57% over two years and 30% over five to six years among contacts. However, the protective effect was observed primarily in the first two years, with no additional effect after four to six years. The GDG emphasized the importance of excluding TB before administering SDR to prevent the emergence of rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Prevention of Leprosy Through Immunoprophylaxis The GDG reviewed evidence on vaccines for leprosy prevention but did not formulate recommendations, as WHO regulations require SAGE to develop all vaccination-related recommendations. Findings on vaccines were shared with the SAGE BCG working group to inform its recommendations. Vaccines remain a critical intervention for leprosy prevention, but further research and guidance are needed.
